title: Spiky QoS probe notes: token-spike drainage experiments
content:
Context / goal:
- Quick exploratory runs to understand how short, high-amplitude token spikes affect latency tail and throughput on dedicated pools. Goal: reproduce 'slow drain' behaviour we saw in Prod on Nov 12 (SRE postmortem), and identify cheap mitigations for customer-facing SLAs.

Hypothesis:
- Short bursts of high-token requests (3x baseline token counts) cause batching to collapse and KV-cache hit rate to drop, producing a bimodal latency distribution (fast small batches vs large single-request runs).
- If batch-formation stalls due to queue prioritization or preemption, GPU utilization remains high but effective throughput drops and P99 explodes.

Environment / setup:
- Cluster: dedicated-squad-A (8xA100-40GB), single-region, on-prem testbed
- Serving runtime commit: 2025-11-14 (sha: f1a2b3c)
- Model: rw-7b-v2 (fp16, no quant) loaded with kv-cache enabled
- Autoscaler: disabled for runs (fixed 8 GPUs)
- Admission policy: default (no token-based admission)
- Traffic generator: custom harness (spike-driver v0.4)
- Observability hooks: token-level traces + batch size histogram + queue depth sampling (5s)

Workload patterns tested:
1) Baseline steady: 450 qps, token distribution mean=32, std=8, 30m run
2) Injected spikes: base 450 qps with a spike pattern every 5m: 30s window where 3x token counts (mean=96), QPS kept constant but per-request tokens increased (simulates expensive prompts)
3) Bursty QPS: short 10s ramp to 2k qps (pure qps spike) — control to separate qps vs token-size effects

Key metrics captured (summary):
- Baseline (steady): throughput=~430 qps (some backpressure), GPU util=74%, batch size median=6, p50=38ms, p95=86ms, p99=210ms
- During token spikes (pattern 2): throughput dropped to ~290 qps for ~45s after injection, GPU util=92% (sustained), batch size median fell to 2, p50=62ms, p95=220ms, p99=1.18s
- During qps-only bursts (pattern 3): throughput saturates GPU, transient p99 ~480ms but recovers to baseline within 20s; batch sizes increased (more small requests batched)

Interpretation / notes:
- Token-increase spikes (same arrival rate but larger token counts) caused the system to process heavier requests singly — batch formation collapsed. That reduced effective throughput while keeping GPUs busy (high util).
- KV cache hit rate dropped ~35% during token spikes (likely due to new prefix tokens and cache eviction from bigger contexts).
- We saw a queue head-of-line effect: long-running requests ended up occupying scheduling slots and subsequent small requests waited, increasing tail latency.
- Difference from qps-only bursts: when QPS increased, batching still worked (many small requests arrived together), so throughput remained closer to capacity; token-size spikes are worse for tail.

Instrumentation snapshots (see dashboard links):
- Batch size histogram shifts left during token spikes (median 6 -> 2).
- Per-GPU kernel time increases, memory spill events (small) observed in logs during 2 of 5 spike windows.
- Queue depth spiked immediately after injection, then slowly drained (~40–50s).

Quick conclusions / actionable ideas:
1) Short-term (low-effort): enable a fast-path admission control that limits tokens-per-minute per-tenant (soft throttling) to avoid single-request monopolies during spikes.
2) Triage: add a limiter on max tokens-per-request in the hosted API (metering + explanation) — for customers that need it, offer chunking helpers in SDK.
3) Runtime change (med-effort): adaptive batching that prefers larger batches over single heavy requests for short windows (i.e., prefer a small wait if it will form a reasonable batch) — needs careful latency SLO tuning.
4) Cache/eviction: prioritize KV cache retention for prefixes that are frequent across short windows; consider tiny local LRU with hotspot pins.
5) Fallbacks: provide a small low-latency model fallback (quantized) for requests exceeding token thresholds so heavy requests are routed to a lane that doesn't block main pool.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How do these effects change with quantized models (4-bit)? run the same pattern on rw-7b-4q to see if batch collapse still occurs or if compute cost reduction helps.
- Is there a correlation between specific prompt structures and cache miss patterns? need token-level diffing across spike windows.
- Can we simulate multi-tenant noise: do spikes from different tenants produce similar drain or is single-tenant spikes worse due to quota/accounting?

Planned next runs:
- Re-run pattern 2 with rw-7b-4q (2025-11-21) and with adaptive-batching flag turned on/off.
- Synthetic test: force artificially slowed kernel (sleep 30–50ms in hot path) to see scheduler sensitivity.
- Run single-tenant vs multi-tenant spike injection to see fairness effects.

Notes to self (scratchpad):
- Capture full flamegraphs for next run; add perf counters to detect memory page faults.
- Talk to SRE (Jonah) about short-term admission control circuit; draft policy to propose to product for hosted guardrails.
- Add a small SDK helper that suggests prompt chunking if token>512 — quick win for UX.

References:
- Internal dashboard snapshots: linked above (DASHBOARD: spiky-qos-2025-11-19)
- Related incident: PROD-2025-11-12-slow-drain postmortem (see Confluence RINF-INC-2025-11-12)

Bottom line: token-size spikes are disproportionately harmful to tail latency because they collapse batching and reduce KV cache effectiveness. Short-term mitigations (admission throttles + SDK helpers) look promising; medium-term fixes require adaptive batching and cache policy work.
